slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: The words boy, girl, city, book, and desk are all names of objects.
Each of these words is a name — and a word that is a name is called a Noun.
We can name a person (John), a place (Chicago), or a thing (railroad).
Whenever we name something we can see or think about, we are using a noun.

slides.heading: Common & Proper Nouns
bullets: A Common Noun fits any one of a whole class:  boy, city, river, dog.
A Proper Noun names one particular person, place, or thing:  John, Chicago, the Mississippi.
Test — “boy” fits every boy, so it is common; “John” names one boy, so it is proper.
Rule — a proper noun always begins with a capital letter (and so do I and O).
A common noun starts with a small letter, unless it begins a sentence.

slides.heading: Practice — Common or Proper?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each noun is common or proper.

slides.heading: Number — One, or More Than One
bullets: Number tells whether a noun means one object or more than one.
Singular Number = one object:  fan, book, boy.
Plural Number = more than one:  fans, books, boys.
We change a noun from singular to plural to speak of many.

slides.heading: Making Plurals
bullets: Most nouns — just add s:  book → books,  girl → girls.
After s, ch, sh, or x — add es:  church → churches,  box → boxes.
y after a consonant — change y to i, add es:  city → cities,  lady → ladies.
Ending in f or fe — often change to ves:  knife → knives,  calf → calves.
A few break the rules:  man → men,  woman → women,  ox → oxen,  sheep → sheep.

slides.heading: Practice — Write the Plurals
slides.instruction: Write the plural of each noun.

slides.heading: Abbreviations
bullets: An Abbreviation is a shortened way of writing a word.
Keep a few letters and put a period at the end:  Doctor → Dr.,  Mister → Mr.
Ex. — Gen. (General),  Mrs. (Mistress),  St. (Saint / Street),  Prof. (Professor).
Ex. — U.S. (United States),  A.M. (before noon),  P.M. (after noon),  No. (Number).
Most abbreviations begin with a capital letter.

slides.heading: Contractions
bullets: A Contraction joins two words and drops some letters.
The apostrophe ( ’ ) marks the spot where letters are left out.
do not → don’t   ·   we are → we’re   ·   I have → I’ve
it is → it’s   ·   they are → they’re   ·   over → o’er
The apostrophe stands in for the missing letters.

slides.heading: Practice — Shortened Words
slides.instruction: Give the full words for each shortened form.

slides.heading: The Parts of a Sentence
bullets: Every sentence affirms something about something.
The Subject is what the sentence is about:  “Ice is cold.” → Ice.
The Predicate is what is affirmed about it:  “Ice is cold.” → cold.
The Copula is the word that links them and makes the assertion:  is.
Copula means “link.” It is usually a form of the verb be — is, was, will be.

slides.heading: Practice — Subject, Predicate, Copula
slides.instruction: Name the subject, predicate, and copula in each sentence.
answers: S: Air · C: is · P: transparent
S: Iron · C: is · P: heavy
S: Nero · C: was · P: cruel
S: Mary · C: should be · P: kind
S: Ellen · C: is · P: unhappy
S: Martha · C: was · P: cheerful

slides.heading: The Predicate & Quality-Words
bullets: The predicate often names a quality of the subject:  “Man is mortal.” → mortal.
Quality-words tell what kind the subject is:  soft, wise, sweet, round, happy.
A noun can be the predicate too — then it tells the class:  “Horses are animals.” → animals.
So a predicate may be a quality (adjective) or a class (noun).

slides.heading: Analysis
bullets: An Element is one distinct part of a sentence.
The Subject and Predicate are the Principal Elements — no sentence can exist without them.
All other parts are Subordinate Elements. (The copula is not counted as an element.)
Analysis means separating a sentence into its elements.
Model — “Iron is heavy.” → Iron | is heavy  (subject | predicate).

slides.heading: Analyze — Diagram the Sentence
slides.instruction: Split each sentence into subject | predicate. The divider after the subject reaches below the baseline.

items: What is the difference between a common and a proper noun?
What does the plural number show?
What are the subject, predicate, and copula?
answers: A word that is a name.
A common noun fits any of a class; a proper noun names one particular thing.
That a noun means more than one object.
A shortened way of writing a word, ending with a period.
The subject is what is spoken of; the predicate is what is affirmed of it; the copula links them.
Separating a sentence into its elements.
